Applied Materials Appoints Akash Palkhiwala to Board of Directors
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Aug. 27, 2026 – Applied Materials, Inc. today announced the appointment of Akash Palkhiwala to serve on its board of directors. As Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operating Officer of Qualcomm Incorporated, Mr. Palkhiwala brings extensive financial and operational leadership experience in the computing and technology industry. Mr. Palkhiwala has also been appointed to the board’s Audit Committee.
“Akash is a terrific addition to our board of directors,” said Tom Iannotti, Chairman of the Board. “His track record of leadership in finance and decades of experience in the semiconductor industry will add to the strength of Applied Materials’ board and serve us well in our next phase of growth.”
Mr. Palkhiwala has served as Qualcomm’s CFO since 2019 and COO since 2024 and is responsible for the finance organization, global go-to-market teams, semiconductor operations and IT. He has also served in various finance leadership roles since joining Qualcomm in 2001. Previously, Mr. Palkhiwala was a private equity analyst at KeyBank.
Mr. Palkhiwala holds an undergraduate degree in mechanical engineering from L.D. College of Engineering in India and an MBA from the University of Maryland.
Applied Materials, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMAT) is the leader in materials engineering solutions that are at the foundation of virtually every new semiconductor and advanced display in the world. The technology we create is essential to advancing AI and accelerating the commercialization of next-generation chips. At Applied, we push the boundaries of science and engineering to deliver material innovation that changes the world. Learn more at www.appliedmaterials.com.

Why Lam Research (LRCX) is Poised to Beat Earnings Estimates Again
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 10:10 AM CDT 3 min read
Looking for a stock that has been consistently beating earnings estimates and might be well positioned to keep the streak alive in its next quarterly report? Lam Research (LRCX), which belongs to the Zacks Electronics - Semiconductors industry, could be a great candidate to consider.
This semiconductor equipment maker has an established record of topping earnings estimates, especially when looking at the previous two reports. The company boasts an average surprise for the past two quarters of 7.89%.
For the most recent quarter, Lam Research was expected to post earnings of $1.69 per share, but it reported $1.82 per share instead, representing a surprise of 7.69%. For the previous quarter, the consensus estimate was $1.36 per share, while it actually produced $1.47 per share, a surprise of 8.09%.
Thanks in part to this history, there has been a favorable change in earnings estimates for Lam Research lately. In fact, the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction) for the stock is positive, which is a great indicator of an earnings beat, particularly when combined with its solid Zacks Rank.
Our research shows that stocks with the combination of a positive Earnings ESP and a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) or better produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time. In other words, if you have 10 stocks with this combination, the number of stocks that beat the consensus estimate could be as high as seven.
The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a version of the Zacks Consensus whose definition is related to change. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.
Lam Research has an Earnings ESP of +2.25% at the moment, suggesting that analysts have grown bullish on its near-term earnings potential. When you combine this positive Earnings ESP with the stock's Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), it shows that another beat is possibly around the corner. The company's next earnings report is expected to be released on October 21, 2026.
Investors should note, however, that a negative Earnings ESP reading is not indicative of an earnings miss, but a negative value does reduce the predictive power of this metric.
Many companies end up beating the consensus EPS estimate, though this is not the only reason why their shares gain. Additionally, some stocks may remain stable even if they end up missing the consensus estimate.
Because of this, it's really important to check a company's Earnings ESP ahead of its quarterly release to increase the odds of success. Make sure to utilize our Earnings ESP Filter to uncover the best stocks to buy or sell before they've reported.

Texas Instruments Faces a Test of Its Own Guidance
Texas Instruments makes analog chips that handle real-world signals like power and temperature. It also makes embedded processors, the small control chips built into machines. On its prior earnings call, Texas Instruments said revenue rose 13% sequentially and 23% year over year. Industrial, data center, and automotive customers led the growth.
Texas Instruments guided third-quarter revenue to $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and EPS to $2.23 to $2.57. The consensus EPS estimate of $2.42 falls inside that range, so the fourth-quarter outlook carries more weight. Management said industrial revenue remains below its 2022 peak and customer inventories have not been rebuilt. Auto demand picked up, led by electric vehicles and hybrids in China. Shares are up 59.2% year to date.
Lam Research Rides AI Demand Into Record Guidance
Lam sells deposition and etch tools, the machines that add and carve away thin layers of material on silicon wafers. On its prior earnings call, Lam said it delivered record revenue, operating margin, and earnings per share “as AI-driven demand continues to reshape the semiconductor industry,” positioning it for “a third consecutive year of outperformance in 2026.”
Lam guided September-quarter revenue to $8.1 billion, plus or minus $400 million, and EPS to $2.15 plus or minus $0.15. It also raised its 2026 forecast for wafer fab equipment spending (what the whole industry spends on chipmaking tools) to the low $150 billion range.
In an August 26 Bloomberg Businessweek report, Lam Research said its advanced packaging business is growing more than 70% year over year. Advanced packaging stacks memory and processor chips in three dimensions and wires them together, so AI hardware works like one large system. Lam shares are down 12.1% over the past week and up 59.0% year to date.
Consensus Points to Steep Year-Over-Year Gains
Jim Cramer described the demand picture on October 19, saying CPUs are “going to be in very short supply, which I think is absolutely true because Taiwan Semi can’t make all the ones that they have.” He added, “There’s tremendous demand, and there’s also an inability to build.” On October 9, he said, “Taiwan Semi controlled pretty much any chip stock.”
When chipmakers cannot build fast enough, they add factory capacity, and that means buying more deposition and etch tools from Lam. Lam said the industry remains meaningfully undersupplied, with several new fabs expected to come online by the end of 2027. The same buildout is pulling in power, cooling, and networking suppliers alongside the chipmakers. (We rounded up seven of those names in a free AI infrastructure report.)
What Each Company Must Prove on Wednesday
Texas Instruments needs a fourth-quarter outlook showing that industrial and automotive demand is still climbing. Lam needs revenue close to its $8.1 billion guidance and more detail on 2027, a year management already called a potentially strong setup.

For months, as energy and food prices surged amid the Iran war, bonds lost their shock-absorber status as investors jacked up estimates of how high interest rates might need to go.
Add near-chronic concern ‌about developed-world governments' finances, and bonds seemed to offer little safe-haven comfort while still struggling to rival super-charged equities.
The correlation between stocks and bond yields has now turned positive for Europe and the U.S., meaning yields are more likely to fall when stocks fall.
It had been overwhelmingly negative this year, with yields rising as stocks fell, undermining bonds' traditional role as a haven during equity selloffs.

Micron vs. Lam Research: Does Buying the Tool Supplier Reduce Memory-Cycle Risk?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 8:57 PM CDT 3 min read
Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) generated $89.68 billion of operating cash in its fiscal year ended September 3. Lam Research Corporation (NASDAQ:LRCX) generated $5.86 billion in its year ended June 28. The relevant question is what remains after investment when those collections weaken. Micron and Lam Research offer different ways to invest in memory demand within our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade. Micron sells memory; Lam supplies manufacturing tools and support. Buying the supplier changes the timing and mechanism of exposure, but it does not escape customers' investment cycles.
How Much Protection Does Micron's Cash Provide in the Next Downturn?
Owning production creates a larger commitment
Micron spent $30.71 billion on property, plant and equipment before government incentives. Lam spent $966 million on capital expenditure and intangible assets. Those investments consumed about 34% and 16% of operating cash, respectively.
Hold those investment bills fixed and reduce operating cash 50%. Micron would retain about $14.13 billion after investment; Lam would retain $1.96 billion. Relative to their respective annual revenue, those residuals equal 10.6% and 8.4%. The larger factory bill does not automatically leave Micron with the weaker current cushion because its starting cash generation is exceptionally high.
Micron's memory prices can change quickly; Lam's equipment orders can respond later and fall sharply when customers postpone capacity. Our Micron liquidity analysis examines why a strong cash balance still needs to be compared with future obligations.
The supplier has more than one source of demand
Lam also serves advanced logic manufacturing, while its support business includes service, spares, upgrades and older-generation tools. That gives it exposure beyond a single memory maker's output. It does not turn the company into a subscription business or guarantee that service collections stay flat during lower factory utilization.
Micron's technology and product mix could sustain stronger economics than older memory cycles suggest. The bear case is that competitive supply eventually catches up with demand, reducing prices while substantial investment continues.
At October 16 equity values, Micron cost about 17 times annual cash after gross capital spending, versus about 68 times for Lam. If Micron's cash after investment fell 75%, its multiple would rise to about 67 at an unchanged share price. That illustrates how much exceptional memory profitability supports the apparent discount; it does not establish that a 75% decline is likely or that equal multiples imply equal value.
Lam's flexibility also depends on capital allocation. Our Lam-Applied payout comparison shows how annual repurchases and dividends can exceed cash left after investment.
Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders rose to 184 from 154 for Micron and to 139 from 123 for Lam. AQR reduced Micron shares 16%, and Arrowstreet reduced Lam shares 7%. Micron's September 30 short interest was 2.31% of float.
Lam reduces direct exposure to memory selling prices and owned-fab spending. Micron starts with a stronger cash yield and a large current funding cushion. The choice depends on confidence in memory economics versus equipment demand; neither company's latest cash flow should be treated as a permanent floor.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of MU and LRCX as investments, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. ASML vs. Lam Research: How Much Protection Does Service Revenue Really Provide?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 1:56 PM CDT 3 min read
ASML Holding N.V. (NASDAQ:ASML) reported about €3.3 billion of installed-base management sales in its September quarter. Lam Research Corporation (NASDAQ:LRCX) reported $2.47 billion of customer-support-related revenue and other in its June quarter. The labels describe different mixtures. ASML and Lam Research both feature in our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade. Both have large businesses supporting equipment already inside chip factories. That can soften a new-equipment slowdown, but calling all of that revenue recurring would give investors too much confidence.
ASML vs. Lam Research: How Much Protection Does Service Revenue Really Provide?
ASML defines installed-base management as net service and field-option sales. Its customers need to maintain costly lithography machines, while upgrades can improve their productivity. Yet upgrades remain spending decisions; the entire category should not be treated as an annually contracted subscription.
Lam's category combines service, spares, upgrades and non-leading-edge Reliant equipment. That last component is equipment sales. The reported support share therefore cannot establish how much purely recurring service revenue Lam has.
Using rounded ASML figures, installed-base sales represented about 28% of quarterly revenue. Lam's broader category represented 36.8%.
Stress the revenue mix, not an invented subscription base
Assume new-system revenue falls 20% while each support category stays flat. ASML's total sales would decline about 14.4%; Lam's would decline 12.6%. If support revenue also falls 10%, the declines become about 17.2% and 16.3%.
Lam's reported mix produces the smaller decline in this exercise, but its equipment content makes a flat support assumption less secure. Neither company discloses enough here to calculate a directly comparable service-only cushion. Lower factory utilization can also reduce demand for spares and usage-related work.
Technology leadership still needs a sensible price
ASML benefits from advanced lithography transitions; Lam benefits from increasingly complex deposition and etch processes. Both face export restrictions and delayed customer investments. Our TSMC-ASML cash comparison explains why a strong cash quarter can also reflect payment timing rather than a permanently larger earnings base.
At October 16 equity values, trailing cash after capital expenditure cost about 26 times for ASML and 68 times for Lam. Working-capital movements make those historical multiples imperfect measures of sustainable cash; the service-mix exercise cannot justify a stock-price target.
Export rules can affect both systems and support. Our ASML geographic-risk analysis explains why a wider customer footprint is not complete protection.
Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders rose to 140 from 133 for ASML and to 139 from 123 for Lam. Fisher increased ASML shares 3%, while Arrowstreet reduced Lam shares 7%. ASML's September 30 short interest was 0.37% of float.
Both installed bases provide business opportunities beyond new-tool shipments. Investors should favor evidence of resilient service collections and profitable upgrades over the largest reported support percentage. Lam's broader category offers a useful buffer, but the disclosures do not establish that it has the stronger recurring-revenue franchise.
While we acknowledge the potential of ASML and LRCX as investments, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Why Lam Research (LRCX) is Poised to Beat Earnings Estimates Again
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 10:10 AM CDT 3 min read
Looking for a stock that has been consistently beating earnings estimates and might be well positioned to keep the streak alive in its next quarterly report? Lam Research (LRCX), which belongs to the Zacks Electronics - Semiconductors industry, could be a great candidate to consider.
This semiconductor equipment maker has an established record of topping earnings estimates, especially when looking at the previous two reports. The company boasts an average surprise for the past two quarters of 7.89%.
For the most recent quarter, Lam Research was expected to post earnings of $1.69 per share, but it reported $1.82 per share instead, representing a surprise of 7.69%. For the previous quarter, the consensus estimate was $1.36 per share, while it actually produced $1.47 per share, a surprise of 8.09%.
Thanks in part to this history, there has been a favorable change in earnings estimates for Lam Research lately. In fact, the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction) for the stock is positive, which is a great indicator of an earnings beat, particularly when combined with its solid Zacks Rank.
Our research shows that stocks with the combination of a positive Earnings ESP and a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) or better produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time. In other words, if you have 10 stocks with this combination, the number of stocks that beat the consensus estimate could be as high as seven.
The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a version of the Zacks Consensus whose definition is related to change. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.
Lam Research has an Earnings ESP of +2.25% at the moment, suggesting that analysts have grown bullish on its near-term earnings potential. When you combine this positive Earnings ESP with the stock's Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), it shows that another beat is possibly around the corner. The company's next earnings report is expected to be released on October 21, 2026.
Investors should note, however, that a negative Earnings ESP reading is not indicative of an earnings miss, but a negative value does reduce the predictive power of this metric.
Many companies end up beating the consensus EPS estimate, though this is not the only reason why their shares gain. Additionally, some stocks may remain stable even if they end up missing the consensus estimate.
Because of this, it's really important to check a company's Earnings ESP ahead of its quarterly release to increase the odds of success. Make sure to utilize our Earnings ESP Filter to uncover the best stocks to buy or sell before they've reported.

Texas Instruments and Lam Research Report Earnings: AI Equipment Boom Meets Analog Rebound
Lam Research and Texas Instruments both report after the close on Wednesday, and each faces a different kind of pressure: one must prove AI equipment demand is still accelerating, while the other needs to show its industrial recovery has real…
Published October 20, 2026, 7:50am ET · 3 min read
Automated robotic arms meticulously assemble electronic components on an advanced manufacturing line, illustrating the high-tech production methods driving growth in the semiconductor industry, particularly for AI equipment and industrial applications. © Shutterstock
Two chip stocks from opposite ends of the industry report on Wednesday, October 21, after the market close. Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX | LRCX Price Prediction) has to show that AI equipment demand is still accelerating. Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) has to show that its industrial and auto rebound can last.
Texas Instruments hosts its call at 3:30 p.m. Central time (4:30 p.m. ET). Lam follows at 5:00 p.m. ET.
Texas Instruments Faces a Test of Its Own Guidance
Texas Instruments makes analog chips that handle real-world signals like power and temperature. It also makes embedded processors, the small control chips built into machines. On its prior earnings call, Texas Instruments said revenue rose 13% sequentially and 23% year over year. Industrial, data center, and automotive customers led the growth.
Texas Instruments guided third-quarter revenue to $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and EPS to $2.23 to $2.57. The consensus EPS estimate of $2.42 falls inside that range, so the fourth-quarter outlook carries more weight. Management said industrial revenue remains below its 2022 peak and customer inventories have not been rebuilt. Auto demand picked up, led by electric vehicles and hybrids in China. Shares are up 59.2% year to date.
Lam Research Rides AI Demand Into Record Guidance
Lam sells deposition and etch tools, the machines that add and carve away thin layers of material on silicon wafers. On its prior earnings call, Lam said it delivered record revenue, operating margin, and earnings per share “as AI-driven demand continues to reshape the semiconductor industry,” positioning it for “a third consecutive year of outperformance in 2026.”
Lam guided September-quarter revenue to $8.1 billion, plus or minus $400 million, and EPS to $2.15 plus or minus $0.15. It also raised its 2026 forecast for wafer fab equipment spending (what the whole industry spends on chipmaking tools) to the low $150 billion range.
In an August 26 Bloomberg Businessweek report, Lam Research said its advanced packaging business is growing more than 70% year over year. Advanced packaging stacks memory and processor chips in three dimensions and wires them together, so AI hardware works like one large system. Lam shares are down 12.1% over the past week and up 59.0% year to date.
Consensus Points to Steep Year-Over-Year Gains
Jim Cramer described the demand picture on October 19, saying CPUs are “going to be in very short supply, which I think is absolutely true because Taiwan Semi can’t make all the ones that they have.” He added, “There’s tremendous demand, and there’s also an inability to build.” On October 9, he said, “Taiwan Semi controlled pretty much any chip stock.”
When chipmakers cannot build fast enough, they add factory capacity, and that means buying more deposition and etch tools from Lam. Lam said the industry remains meaningfully undersupplied, with several new fabs expected to come online by the end of 2027. The same buildout is pulling in power, cooling, and networking suppliers alongside the chipmakers. (We rounded up seven of those names in a free AI infrastructure report.)
What Each Company Must Prove on Wednesday
Texas Instruments needs a fourth-quarter outlook showing that industrial and automotive demand is still climbing. Lam needs revenue close to its $8.1 billion guidance and more detail on 2027, a year management already called a potentially strong setup.

To own Lam Research, you need to believe that AI, 5G and advanced automotive chips keep requiring fresh wafer capacity, and that Lam keeps winning a healthy share of those etch and deposition budgets. The recent record US$6.72b quarter and stronger guidance support that view, although they do not remove the cyclicality of wafer fab equipment spending.
In the short term, the key catalyst is whether that AI driven order visibility actually converts into sustained tool shipments and service revenue. This is particularly important as export controls and a higher tax rate start to bite. The biggest operational risk is still regional and policy exposure, especially any slowdown in non China fab projects as China becomes a smaller share of revenue.
The most relevant recent development is Lam Research's record Q2 performance, with US$6.72b in quarterly revenue, 30% higher year on year, and earnings per share plus forward guidance ahead of analyst expectations. This result matters because it ties Lam's tools directly to AI and complex memory capacity, turning chipmakers' long build cycles into clearer multi quarter demand signals.
For you as a shareholder, that update feeds straight into the core catalysts. AI capex is linked by management to wafer fab equipment demand, while a growing installed base supports the Customer Support Business Group, which already runs near US$2.5b a quarter. Execution risk now sits in delivering tools to those 8 to 10 planned Tier 1 fabs while managing export limits and a structurally higher tax bill.
Lam Research's current analyst narrative points to revenues of US$46.4b and earnings of US$17.7b by 2029, based on assumed yearly top line growth of 25.9%. That path starts from earnings today of US$7.3b and implies an earnings increase of about US$10.4b over the period, with consensus estimates focused on 2029 as the key forecast year.

Q2 Rundown: Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) Vs Other Semiconductor Manufacturing Stocks
Earnings results often indicate what direction a company will take in the months ahead. With Q2 behind us, let's have a look at Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) and its peers.
The semiconductor industry is driven by demand for advanced electronic products like smartphones, PCs, servers, and data storage. The need for technologies like artificial intelligence, 5G networks, and smart cars is also creating the next wave of growth for the industry. Keeping up with this dynamism requires new tools that can design, fabricate, and test chips at ever smaller sizes and more complex architectures, creating a dire need for semiconductor capital manufacturing equipment.
The 14 semiconductor manufacturing stocks we track reported a very strong Q2. As a group, revenues beat analysts' consensus estimates by 3.5% while next quarter's revenue guidance was 6.5% above.
Amidst this news, share prices of the companies have had a rough stretch. On average, they are down 7.5% since the latest earnings results.
Founded in 1980 by David Lam, the man who pioneered semiconductor etching technology, Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) is one of the leading providers of wafer fabrication equipment used to make semiconductors.
Lam Research reported revenues of $6.72 billion, up 30% year on year. This print was in line with analysts' expectations, and overall, it was an exceptional quarter for the company with a beat of analysts' EPS estimates and revenue guidance for next quarter exceeding analysts' expectations.
"Lam delivered record revenue, operating margin and earnings per share in the June quarter as AI-driven demand continues to reshape the semiconductor industry," said Tim Archer, Lam Research's President and Chief Executive Officer.
Interestingly, the stock is up 4.9% since reporting and currently trades at $264.60.
We think Lam Research is a good business, but is it a buy today? Read our full report here, it's free.
Best Q2: Kulicke and Soffa (NASDAQ:KLIC)
Headquartered in Singapore, Kulicke & Soffa (NASDAQ: KLIC) is a provider of production equipment and tools used to assemble semiconductor devices
Kulicke and Soffa reported revenues of $330.4 million, up 123% year on year, outperforming analysts' expectations by 5.7%. The business had a stunning quarter with a significant improvement in its inventory levels and a beat of analysts' EPS estimates.
Kulicke and Soffa pulled off the fastest revenue growth of the whole group. Although it had a fine quarter compared to its peers, the market seems unhappy with the results as the stock is down 16.4% since reporting. It currently trades at $78.50.
Is now the time to buy Kulicke and Soffa? Access our full analysis of the earnings results here, it's free.
Weakest Q2: KLA Corporation (NASDAQ:KLAC)
Formed by the 1997 merger of the two leading semiconductor yield management companies, KLA Corporation (NASDAQ:KLAC) is the leading supplier of equipment used to measure and inspect semiconductor chips.
KLA Corporation reported revenues of $3.66 billion, up 15.2% year on year, exceeding analysts' expectations by 1.3%. It may have had the worst quarter among its peers, but its results were still good as it also locked in a beat of analysts' EPS estimates and a decent beat of analysts' operating income estimates.
As expected, the stock is down 12.7% since the results and currently trades at $166.66.
Read our full analysis of KLA Corporation's results here.
Headquartered in Israel, Nova (NASDAQ:NVMI) is a provider of quality control systems used in semiconductor manufacturing.
Nova reported revenues of $255 million, up 15.9% year on year. This number surpassed analysts' expectations by 1.6%. Overall, it was a very strong quarter as it also put up a significant improvement in its inventory levels and an impressive beat of analysts' operating income estimates.
The stock is down 19.9% since reporting and currently trades at $322.22.
Read our full, actionable report on Nova here, it's free.
Sporting a global footprint of facilities, Photronics (NASDAQ:PLAB) is a manufacturer of photomasks, templates used to transfer patterns onto semiconductor wafers.
Photronics reported revenues of $216 million, up 2.7% year on year. This result topped analysts' expectations by 3.5%. It was an exceptional quarter as it also produced a beat of analysts' EPS estimates and an impressive beat of analysts' operating income estimates.
Photronics had the slowest revenue growth in the group. The stock is down 6.5% since reporting and currently trades at $27.40.
Read our full, actionable report on Photronics here, it's free.
Over the past year, investors have been forced to repeatedly answer the same question: what is the market's biggest risk? The answer has changed several times, and each shift has reshaped market leadership.
Late in 2025 and early 2026, artificial intelligence became the market's primary uncertainty. Investors questioned whether AI would erode software pricing power and weaken competitive moats as AI made it easier to replicate once-differentiated products.
By the spring, technology took a back seat to geopolitics. The U.S. conflict with Iran briefly became the market's dominant narrative, raising concerns about oil prices, inflation, and global growth. But as energy markets remained orderly and fears of a prolonged supply disruption faded, investors quickly turned their focus back to fundamentals.

Chicago, IL – October 20, 2026 – Zacks.com announces the list of stocks featured in the Analyst Blog. Stocks recently featured in the blog include: Meta Platforms META, Lam Research LRCX, Texas Instruments TXN, Tesla TSLA, Netflix NFLX, Procter & Gamble PG and GE Aerospace GE.
Here are highlights from Monday's Analyst Blog:
Q3 Earnings Reports Gear Up: Global Week Ahead
What happens across this Global Week Ahead?
· Q3 earnings season is shifting up a gear in the U.S., and
· Mainland China is about to deliver a deluge of macro data
· Giving febrile markets plenty more to ponder after the latest bouts of volatility in bonds and AI stocks
Elsewhere:
· Central bankers in Indonesia and Turkey have been given headaches by global index provider MSCI, while
· Voters in Brazil gear up to choose their next president
Next are Reuters' five world market themes, re-ordered for equity traders—
U.S. earnings season picks up in the coming days, with investors focused on Meta Platforms and other AI-focused companies as technology shares wobble.
Meta, due on Wednesday, is one of several hyper-scalers whose massive spending on AI data centers and infrastructure has been a big driver of investment.
With concerns mounting over financing for the AI buildout, investors want more detail on expected returns from those huge outlays.
Reports from semiconductor companies Lam Research and Texas Instruments will offer another view of the AI boom, as will results from Elon Musk's Tesla.
Other high-profile results in the coming days include Netflix, Procter & Gamble and GE Aerospace.
S&P500 earnings are expected to have climbed more than +30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES, continuing a robust year for corporate profits.
(2) Stock & Bond Returns Correlation a Focus
For months, as energy and food prices surged amid the Iran war, bonds lost their shock-absorber status as investors jacked up estimates of how high interest rates might need to go.
Add near-chronic concern ‌about developed-world governments' finances, and bonds seemed to offer little safe-haven comfort while still struggling to rival super-charged equities.
The correlation between stocks and bond yields has now turned positive for Europe and the U.S., meaning yields are more likely to fall when stocks fall.
It had been overwhelmingly negative this year, with yields rising as stocks fell, undermining bonds' traditional role as a haven during equity selloffs.
This relationship fluctuates, but this year, the correlation of U.S. stocks and bond yields in March hit its most negative since at least the 1990s, while for European assets, it reached its most negative on record in September.
(3) MSCI Proposed Stripping Indonesia of EM Status. Turkey Put on Notice, Too
Central bankers in Indonesia and Turkey already have plenty on their plates.
Now they have an MSCI headache, too.
Indonesia's central bank meets on Wednesday, while Turkish policymakers gather on Thursday, against a backdrop of high energy prices, rising borrowing costs, AI-driven market disruption and geopolitical uncertainty.
MSCI has proposed stripping Indonesia of its emerging-market (EM) status and removing it from a suite of indexes, a move that risks triggering heavy outflows and raising pressure on policymakers to hike from 5.75% rather than hold.
MSCI has also put Turkey on notice, warning of a potential downgrade if market reforms fall short by mid-2027, another complication for policymakers expected to keep cutting rates from 37%.
(4) The Week Starts with a Mainland China Macro Data Deluge
A health check on the Chinese economy is due on Monday, with third-quarter GDP alongside September retail sales, industrial output and fixed-asset investment data.
The latest loan prime rate follows on Tuesday and is expected to stay put after more than a year on hold.
Strong global demand for semiconductors, clean technology and other manufactured goods has kept China's economy ticking, even as domestic demand remains patchy and higher energy costs bite.
Exports have held up despite China's delicate trade balancing act with the U.S. and E.U.
The latest trade figures showed Chinese exports surging well beyond analysts' estimates, putting the country on track for another $1 trillion trade surplus this year after crossing the threshold for the first time in 2025.
The flip side: the export boom could add to trade tensions with major partners.
(4) Brazil's Presidential Runoff Happens on October 25th. Campaigning Underway
Brazil's October 25th presidential runoff is keeping markets on edge after Flávio Bolsonaro's surprise first-round lead sent stocks up 7.7% and the real almost 4% higher.
A new Quaest poll puts Bolsonaro on 46% versus Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's 44%, a technical tie.
Investors are betting a Bolsonaro win would bring tighter fiscal policy, but much may already be priced in. His choice of economic team and signs of credible reform could fuel further gains.
A Lula comeback, meanwhile, could put that rally into reverse, with the real, longer-dated bonds and state-controlled companies among the most exposed. A more conservative Congress, though, could limit how far Lula could shift policy.

Micron vs. Lam Research: Does Buying the Tool Supplier Reduce Memory-Cycle Risk?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 8:57 PM CDT 3 min read
Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) generated $89.68 billion of operating cash in its fiscal year ended September 3. Lam Research Corporation (NASDAQ:LRCX) generated $5.86 billion in its year ended June 28. The relevant question is what remains after investment when those collections weaken. Micron and Lam Research offer different ways to invest in memory demand within our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade. Micron sells memory; Lam supplies manufacturing tools and support. Buying the supplier changes the timing and mechanism of exposure, but it does not escape customers' investment cycles.
How Much Protection Does Micron's Cash Provide in the Next Downturn?
Owning production creates a larger commitment
Micron spent $30.71 billion on property, plant and equipment before government incentives. Lam spent $966 million on capital expenditure and intangible assets. Those investments consumed about 34% and 16% of operating cash, respectively.
Hold those investment bills fixed and reduce operating cash 50%. Micron would retain about $14.13 billion after investment; Lam would retain $1.96 billion. Relative to their respective annual revenue, those residuals equal 10.6% and 8.4%. The larger factory bill does not automatically leave Micron with the weaker current cushion because its starting cash generation is exceptionally high.
Micron's memory prices can change quickly; Lam's equipment orders can respond later and fall sharply when customers postpone capacity. Our Micron liquidity analysis examines why a strong cash balance still needs to be compared with future obligations.
The supplier has more than one source of demand
Lam also serves advanced logic manufacturing, while its support business includes service, spares, upgrades and older-generation tools. That gives it exposure beyond a single memory maker's output. It does not turn the company into a subscription business or guarantee that service collections stay flat during lower factory utilization.
Micron's technology and product mix could sustain stronger economics than older memory cycles suggest. The bear case is that competitive supply eventually catches up with demand, reducing prices while substantial investment continues.
At October 16 equity values, Micron cost about 17 times annual cash after gross capital spending, versus about 68 times for Lam. If Micron's cash after investment fell 75%, its multiple would rise to about 67 at an unchanged share price. That illustrates how much exceptional memory profitability supports the apparent discount; it does not establish that a 75% decline is likely or that equal multiples imply equal value.
Lam's flexibility also depends on capital allocation. Our Lam-Applied payout comparison shows how annual repurchases and dividends can exceed cash left after investment.
Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders rose to 184 from 154 for Micron and to 139 from 123 for Lam. AQR reduced Micron shares 16%, and Arrowstreet reduced Lam shares 7%. Micron's September 30 short interest was 2.31% of float.
Lam reduces direct exposure to memory selling prices and owned-fab spending. Micron starts with a stronger cash yield and a large current funding cushion. The choice depends on confidence in memory economics versus equipment demand; neither company's latest cash flow should be treated as a permanent floor.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of MU and LRCX as investments, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. ASML vs. Lam Research: How Much Protection Does Service Revenue Really Provide?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 1:56 PM CDT 3 min read
ASML Holding N.V. (NASDAQ:ASML) reported about €3.3 billion of installed-base management sales in its September quarter. Lam Research Corporation (NASDAQ:LRCX) reported $2.47 billion of customer-support-related revenue and other in its June quarter. The labels describe different mixtures. ASML and Lam Research both feature in our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade. Both have large businesses supporting equipment already inside chip factories. That can soften a new-equipment slowdown, but calling all of that revenue recurring would give investors too much confidence.
ASML vs. Lam Research: How Much Protection Does Service Revenue Really Provide?
ASML defines installed-base management as net service and field-option sales. Its customers need to maintain costly lithography machines, while upgrades can improve their productivity. Yet upgrades remain spending decisions; the entire category should not be treated as an annually contracted subscription.
Lam's category combines service, spares, upgrades and non-leading-edge Reliant equipment. That last component is equipment sales. The reported support share therefore cannot establish how much purely recurring service revenue Lam has.
Using rounded ASML figures, installed-base sales represented about 28% of quarterly revenue. Lam's broader category represented 36.8%.
Stress the revenue mix, not an invented subscription base
Assume new-system revenue falls 20% while each support category stays flat. ASML's total sales would decline about 14.4%; Lam's would decline 12.6%. If support revenue also falls 10%, the declines become about 17.2% and 16.3%.
Lam's reported mix produces the smaller decline in this exercise, but its equipment content makes a flat support assumption less secure. Neither company discloses enough here to calculate a directly comparable service-only cushion. Lower factory utilization can also reduce demand for spares and usage-related work.
Technology leadership still needs a sensible price
ASML benefits from advanced lithography transitions; Lam benefits from increasingly complex deposition and etch processes. Both face export restrictions and delayed customer investments. Our TSMC-ASML cash comparison explains why a strong cash quarter can also reflect payment timing rather than a permanently larger earnings base.
At October 16 equity values, trailing cash after capital expenditure cost about 26 times for ASML and 68 times for Lam. Working-capital movements make those historical multiples imperfect measures of sustainable cash; the service-mix exercise cannot justify a stock-price target.
Export rules can affect both systems and support. Our ASML geographic-risk analysis explains why a wider customer footprint is not complete protection.
Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders rose to 140 from 133 for ASML and to 139 from 123 for Lam. Fisher increased ASML shares 3%, while Arrowstreet reduced Lam shares 7%. ASML's September 30 short interest was 0.37% of float.
Both installed bases provide business opportunities beyond new-tool shipments. Investors should favor evidence of resilient service collections and profitable upgrades over the largest reported support percentage. Lam's broader category offers a useful buffer, but the disclosures do not establish that it has the stronger recurring-revenue franchise.
While we acknowledge the potential of ASML and LRCX as investments, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Fri, October 16, 2026 at 7:15 AM CDT 2 min read
Wall Street analysts forecast that Lam Research (LRCX) will report quarterly earnings of $2.17 per share in its upcoming release, pointing to a year-over-year increase of 72.2%. It is anticipated that revenues will amount to $8.12 billion, exhibiting an increase of 52.4% compared to the year-ago quarter.
Over the last 30 days, there has been an upward revision of 0.4% in the consensus EPS estimate for the quarter, leading to its current level. This signifies the covering analysts' collective reconsideration of their initial forecasts over the course of this timeframe.
Before a company announces its earnings, it is essential to take into account any changes made to earnings estimates. This is a valuable factor in predicting the potential reactions of investors toward the stock. Empirical research has consistently shown a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and the short-term price performance of a stock.
While investors typically use consensus earnings and revenue estimates as a yardstick to evaluate the company's quarterly performance, scrutinizing analysts' projections for some of the company's key metrics can offer a more comprehensive perspective.
In light of this perspective, let's dive into the average estimates of certain Lam Research metrics that are commonly tracked and forecasted by Wall Street analysts.
The consensus estimate for 'Revenue- Customer support-related revenue and other' stands at $2.50 billion. The estimate indicates a change of +40.6% from the prior-year quarter.
The collective assessment of analysts points to an estimated 'Revenue- Systems' of $5.61 billion. The estimate points to a change of +58.3% from the year-ago quarter.
Analysts predict that the 'Leading- and non-leading-edge equipment and upgrade Revenue - Memory' will reach 45.7%. The estimate is in contrast to the year-ago figure of 34.0%.
The average prediction of analysts places 'Leading- and non-leading-edge equipment and upgrade Revenue - Logic/integrated device manufacturing' at 10.7%. The estimate compares to the year-ago value of 6.0%.

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.
Chipmaking-equipment supplier Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) traded at $263.48, down approximately 3.20%, on October 20, as investors weighed valuation ahead of its next earnings report. The earlier quote was recorded at 11.34 a.m. ET; the updated price has no specified intraday timestamp. The Fly reported that Evercore ISI lowered its price target to $315 from $355 while keeping an Outperform rating. That leaves a bullish recommendation with a smaller cushion.

The cash numbers deserve attention. Lam's June-quarter release showed operating cash flow of $1.457 billion against net income of $2.277 billionroughly 64% conversion by calculation. Receivables climbed 29.2% sequentially to $5.340 billion, outpacing revenue growth of 15.1%. More sales were sitting in unpaid customer balances at quarter-end. That warrants scrutiny, but does not establish collection trouble or fading demand. Jul 29, 2026
The valuation graphic adds pressure: shares stand 64.59% above the $160.08 GF Value estimate, suggesting substantial expectations are already priced in. That estimate is a benchmark, not a guaranteed destination. My next checkpoint is simple: can cash collections catch up with sales? Stronger operating cash flow and slower receivables growth would help support the premium. Another quarter of earnings racing ahead of cash would leave investors with more questions.

In other words, if you have 10 stocks with this combination, the number of stocks that beat the consensus estimate could be as high as seven. The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a version of the Zacks Consensus whose definition is related to change. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier. Lam Research has an Earnings ESP of +2.25% at the moment, suggesting that analysts have grown bullish on its near-term earnings potential. Netflix's third-quarter earnings failed to excite investors, a week after a major content executive shuffle and its biggest round of layoffs since 2022.
The streamer turned in results above expectations for the third quarter, but provided weak guidance for the rest of the year. Netflix said its earnings beat was primarily due to the timing of expenses.
Netflix's revenue growth slowed for a third straight quarter, and the company projected it would continue to decelerate in the fourth quarter.

The streaming leader cut its annual advertising forecast from $3 billion to $2.7 billion, citing a slower-than-expected rollout of its ad products.

Netflix said in its third-quarter shareholder letter that it knows "there's some investor concern about our view hours growth" but added that engagement "remains healthy."
"We do seek to accelerate growth in view hours as well, and we're confident we'll do that by relentlessly focusing and executing" its strategy, the shareholder letter said.
The company has invested in video games and podcasts but didn't mention either in its letter, outside a disclosure section on "forward-looking statements."
Netflix's results came less than a week after it shook up its content leadership team and cut about 1,000 workers.

"It's our goal to go from very good to great," co-CEO Greg Peters said of Netflix's content slate on the company's earnings call.

Netflix shares drop on slowing engagement, revenue growth
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 5:41 PM CDT 3 min read
California-based streaming giant Netflix saw shares drop amid concerns about a slowdown in viewer engagement and revenue growth (JUSTIN SULLIVAN)
Netflix stock dropped more than five percent Tuesday afternoon after its quarterly earnings release failed to assuage investor concerns about a slowdown in viewer engagement and revenue growth.
"We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," the company said in a letter to investors, referring to how the company measures engagement, and added that it was "confident" it could accelerate that growth.
The California-based streaming giant has struggled to meet investor expectations for several quarters as it faces competition from other streamers, gaming and sports.
Netflix "has underperformed significantly over the last 6-12 months" and investors are concerned "about soft engagement trends, decelerating revenue growth, a slower margin expansion outlook, and most recently content executive leadership changes," John Belton, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, told AFP in a statement.
In its third quarter ending in September, Netflix recorded $12.87 billion in revenue and $3.7 billion in net income, above investor expectations, according to FactSet.
It did not provide overall figures for subscriber view hours in the quarter, but noted that in India the metric increased 24 percent compared to the same period last year.
In July, Netflix said subscribers spent 97 billion hours watching content in the first half of the year, a 2 percent increase over the first half of 2025.
It stopped reporting subscriber numbers in the first half of 2025.
But the company touted growth outside the US while acknowledging challenges stateside.
"We do need better execution in the U.S. Our content around the world is largely working," co-CEO Ted Sarandos told investors on an analyst call Tuesday, highlighting engagement, subscribers, revenue and profits across Latin America, Europe and Asia.
"The U.S. is also working. It's just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like," Sarandos continued.
The company will also reportedly cut around 6 percent of its workforce, or 1,000 jobs, according to media reports.
Among them were seven high-level employees in charge of television deals and content, the Hollywood Reporter reported last week.
The company also recently replaced chief content officer Bela Bajaria, who oversaw popular shows including "Stranger Things," "Bridgerton," and "Squid Game," in addition to pushing the company's live entertainment strategy, according to CNBC.
Netflix appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice to be its new content chief.
"Peter Rice understands talent relations, and in a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work," Sarandos said on the call Tuesday.
Competition from other streamers has forced Netflix to work harder to attract and retain both paid and ad-supported members.
The company has increasingly dipped into live sports -- with agreements to stream major events like the Olympics and World Cup -- in addition to gaming and shorter-form content. The NFL and WWE are also on board to stream live events.
In the US, it reached 7.8 percent of streaming television viewers in July compared to YouTube's 14.2 percent, a record for the Google-owned site, according to media analytics firm Nielsen.
The World Cup lifted overall television viewership in July, according to Nielsen.
"It's really important to remember, roughly 95 percent of our spend and nearly all of our revenue is focused on that core, where we see a long runway for future growth," Sarandos said on Tuesday's call, emphasizing its commitment to traditional television and film content.
The company also missed expectations on advertising revenue growth.
"We are currently a bit behind our aggressive target for the year. We're still growing" on advertising, nonetheless, co-CEO Greg Peters said on the call.
"We see the benefits when we continue to roll out other products like new ad formats, which help with our growth," Peters added.

Third-quarter results from Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX | NFLX Price Prediction) are due on October 20 after the close. Shares head in at $70.53. The 24/7 Wall St. price target for Netflix is $81.75, which means 15.91% upside. The stock earns a buy rating with high confidence from the model.
Price Target from 24/7 Wall St.
Wall Street leans the same way. Netflix has 7 Strong Buy, 28 Buy, 15 Hold and 1 Sell ratings, and the consensus target is $91.39.
Management guided Q3 to revenue of $12.86B and EPS of $0.82. Consensus stands at $0.8229 and $12.88 billion, so Netflix needs a clean beat on both lines.
A 40% Slide Sets a Low Bar Heading Into Earnings
Over the past year the stock has lost 40.41%, including a 24.78% drop year to date and a 7.7% decline over the past month. It is up 0.33% for the week. That leaves shares much closer to the $65.08 52-week low than to the $124.86 high. On Friday the stock fell 2.86% after Netflix, a Walt Disney (NYSE:DIS) rival, replaced its content chief with a former Disney executive.
In Q2, revenue grew 13.4% to $12.56B, slightly missing expectations. EPS of $0.80 came in ahead of the $0.79 consensus. Even so, shares fell 7.26% on the day. This stock has been punished hard for misses, with an average response of -9.89%.
Our one-year bull case is $119.90. Advertising is expected to roughly double to about $3B in 2026. Management says the revenue gap between the ad tier and the ad-free plan “is narrowing.”
Netflix also has $27.1B left on its buyback authorizations, and it reaches less than 45% of an estimated 800 million addressable households. Full-year guidance still calls for operating margin of 31.5%.

Netflix Earns a Premium Over Its Streaming Rivals
Disney is the most direct competitor in streaming, and Disney+ and Hulu SVOD operating income more than doubled to $712 million last quarter. Disney trades at a lower multiple, though its operating margin is roughly half of Netflix’s.
Spotify Technology (NYSE:SPOT) runs a similar subscription-plus-ads model and grew revenue 13.93%, about the same rate as Netflix, yet it trades at nearly twice Netflix’s multiple.
Netflix pairs the best margins in this group with a mid-range multiple, so the comparison makes the 24/7 Wall St. price target look reasonable, arguably conservative.

Netflix (NFLX -1.66%) released third-quarter earnings after hours on Tuesday, and it was another disappointment for investors. The stock was trading down 6% after hours.
While its headline numbers were slightly ahead of expectations, Netflix's engagement remained weak, and its trend of slowing growth continued. In fact, the company reported its slowest top-line growth in three years, and it expects it to continue to moderate in the fourth quarter.
Overall revenue rose 11.8% to $12.87 billion, which matched expectations, while its operating margin came in at 34% due to the timing of its content spend. On the bottom line, earnings per share improved from $0.59 to $0.87, beating estimates of $0.82.
However, beyond the existing concerns about engagement and its weak original content slate, one number underscored Netflix's troubles. The company cut its ad revenue guidance for the year from $3 billion to $2.7 billion, indicating weakness in what's supposed to be a key growth market for the streamer.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
Netflix was late to launch its advertising business, finally pulling the trigger in 2022 after years of resistance. The decision has turned out to be a success, giving customers a lower-priced option and allowing advertisers to meet audiences where they are, on streaming. The two-tiered advertising model has become the norm in the streaming industry, and all of Netflix's rivals offer some version of a higher-priced ad-free tier and a lower-priced tier with ads.
Advertising was also supposed to give Netflix an avenue for growth at a time when its subscription business is believed to be maturing, especially in core markets like the U.S. Netflix no longer reports quarterly subscriber numbers, so investors don't have much insight into subscriber growth anymore.
Netflix cut its ad revenue forecast due to a "slightly slower than expected rollout of some ad product capabilities," which places the blame for the shortfall on a technical issue rather than a business issue like weak demand from advertisers or poor engagement. That's a good sign for investors, but still a disappointment, nonetheless.
Is it a red flag?
Advertising still makes up a small fraction of Netflix's revenue. The streamer expects to bring in $51.1 billion in revenue this year, meaning that advertising makes up less than 6% of its revenue. The subscription business still dominates.
However, advertising is a key part of the growth story, and it could face increased scrutiny from Wall Street, especially given the disappointing engagement trends.
The advertising weakness isn't a red flag, but Netflix has become a "show-me story" this year, meaning it needs to prove to investors that it can stop its growth slowdown and improve engagement, or it will continue to face skepticism, which is likely to push the stock lower. The advertising weakness, whether it's due to a one-off technical issue or something else, only adds to those concerns.

That's still decent top-line growth, but the company desperately needs to show Wall Street that something is going right for the business, or the stock slide looks likely to continue. At one point, advertising looked like that bright spot, but unless management tells us something different in the fourth-quarter report, investors may count that as another one of many disappointments from the company over the last year.

Netflix (NFLX) Stock Nears Earnings With $64–$77 Range in Focus
Netflix stock faces a key earnings test Tuesday as options signal wide price swings and analysts track revenue growth ahead of Q3.
By Maxwell MutumaOctober 19, 2026No Comments3 Mins Read
Netflix shares have fallen nearly 47% from their June 2025 peak, ahead of Tuesday’s earnings.
Options markets suggest Netflix stock could move approximately 9% following the third-quarter results.
BMO Capital Markets and Wedbush lowered their Netflix stock price targets before the earnings release.
Analysts expect Netflix revenue to reach $12.87 billion, with earnings of approximately $0.82 per share.
Netflix faces slower revenue growth as advertising, subscription pricing and streaming competition remain in focus.
Netflix (NFLX) shares face a test on Tuesday, October 20, when the streaming company reports third-quarter earnings. The stock closed Friday at $70.53, almost 47% below its June 2025 peak, as investors weighed slower growth and stronger competition.
Netflix Options Point to Another Price Swing
Traders expect a sharp move after the results. Short-dated options have shown implied volatility near 92.3%, compared with historical volatility of about 34%, reflecting higher prices for protection against sudden share movements.
Market estimates indicate that Netflix shares could move roughly 9% in either direction after earnings. That would place the stock near $64 or $77.
Options data also showed more calls than puts, with a reported put-to-call ratio below 0.40. Such positioning indicates demand for upside exposure, although it cannot establish which direction the stock will move.
Analysts Lower Netflix Stock Price Targets
Several analysts adjusted forecasts before the report. BMO Capital Markets reduced its price target to $125 from $135 while keeping an outperform rating. Wedbush lowered its target from $105 to $90.
Jefferies set an $85 target with a buy rating, while Huber Research downgraded the shares to sell and set a $70 target. Analysts remain divided over how quickly Netflix can increase viewing and advertising revenue.
Audience trends across digital media have also faced scrutiny. Recent Truth Social traffic estimates pointed to fewer daily users, although the figures concern a separate platform and do not measure Netflix viewing.
Analysts expect third-quarter revenue of approximately $12.87 billion, up nearly 12% from a year earlier. They forecast earnings of 82 cents per share, compared with 59 cents in the previous year.
Netflix generated $12.56 billion in second-quarter revenue, representing 13% annual growth. It now expects full-year sales between $51 billion and $51.4 billion and has projected advertising revenue near $3 billion in 2026.
Competition extends beyond subscription services. A recent streaming distribution agreement involving FreeCast shows how other providers are seeking viewers through bundled entertainment and advertising-supported programming.
Technology spending remains another industry focus. Meta’s recent AI model release came as Netflix continued using technology in content production and advertising, although their initiatives serve different purposes.

After establishing the business through a commercial representation model, which was instrumental in building its presence in Brazil, Netflix will work more closely with licensees through a larger local team dedicated to faster decision-making, with a focus on relevance, engagement and innovation.
In practice, direct relationships will evolve the way products are developed. Partners will be able to tell Netflix directly which audiences, categories or cultural conversations they want to explore. Netflix, in turn, will identify opportunities through its knowledge of fandoms: the most talked-about characters, what went viral in the previous season and what fans want more of.

To support this new phase, the local team is expanding with specialists in creative development and projects integrated with the advertising business, which works directly with Netflix’s ad-supported plan, and brand partnerships, which develops brand campaigns on and off the screen. Both are part of the company’s commercial ecosystem, alongside consumer products.
For brands, this connection offers a way to participate in cultural universes where passion and demand already exist, driving sales and brand recall. That potential is an expression of the Netflix Effect: the ability of stories to shape culture, influence behavior and generate demand beyond the screen. With “KPop Demon Hunters,” that interest translated into products ranging from toys to food, with partners such as Candide, Grow, C&A, Renner, Riachuelo, Ediouro, Grendene, Tilibra and Knorr, alongside global brands available in the country. Streaming major trims 2026 ad revenue forecast to $2.7 billion as slower growth and US content execution weigh on investor sentiment, viewing hours rise 24% in India
Published:
Netflix reported a 44% year-on-year increase in third-quarter profit and an 11.8% rise in revenue, marking the lowest growth rate in three years, but issued a weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter earnings outlook, leading to a nearly 6% drop in shares.
The company lowered its 2026 advertising revenue forecast from $3 billion to approximately $2.7 billion, citing delays in product rollouts and partner integrations, despite expecting over 80% growth in its advertising business this year.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos emphasized the need for better execution in the U.S. market and highlighted the importance of producing quality content to enhance subscriber engagement amid increasing competition from platforms like YouTube and TikTok.
Netflix experienced a 24% increase in viewing hours in India during the third quarter, driven by successful local content, and reported its largest quarter of paid net additions in the region.
Netflix’s third-quarter profit rose 44% year-on-year and revenue jumped 11.8% (lowest rate of increase in 3 years), but its weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter earnings outlook and a reduction in its full-year advertising revenue forecast triggered a fresh sell-off in its shares on Tuesday, highlighting the pressure to sustain growth as it scales up its advertising business.
Netflix reduced its advertising forecast for 2026 to roughly $2.7 billion, down from about $3 billion. Some ad product capabilities rolled out slightly slower than expected, executives said in their quarterly letter to shareholders.
Shares fell nearly 6% to $64.66 in after-hours trading on October 20. The stock had already lost more than 25% of its value over the preceding year, reflecting concerns about engagement growth, competition and the sustainability of its premium valuation.
"I know that we could do better," Co-CEO Ted Sarandos said in a post-earnings video call. "Now we've seen an opportunity to take our slate to the next level."
Third-quarter revenue rose 11.8% to $12.87 billion, in line with Wall Street forecasts, but the lowest rate of increase in nearly ⁠three years. The company forecast fourth-quarter net income of $2.79 billion and EPS of 67 cents, below the average analyst forecast of $3.07 billion and 73 cents.
Sarandos said the company plans to focus on its core business of producing quality TV shows and movies to make Netflix a must-have service, and the recent executive shakeup was a step toward that goal. In its earnings report, Netflix said it would continue to expand its offerings through licensing more third-party ‌content.
Netflix expects fourth-quarter revenue of $13.44 billion, up 11.5% year-on-year, but forecasts net income of $2.79 billion and earnings per share of 67 cents. Both figures fall short of analysts’ expectations of $3.07 billion and 73 cents, respectively. The company also projects an operating margin of 26%, down from 34.6% in Q3.
For the full year, Netflix maintained its revenue guidance of $51.1 billion, representing approximately 13% growth, and an operating margin target of 31.5%. However, it lowered its 2026 advertising revenue forecast to approximately $2.7 billion from $3 billion, citing delays in rolling out advertising products and partner integrations. Despite the revision, the advertising business is expected to grow more than 80% this year, according to co-CEO Greg Peters.
For advertisers and media buyers, the revision highlights the difference between growing demand for streaming inventory and building the technology, partnerships and formats needed to monetise it at scale.
Sarandos calls for stronger US content execution
Sarandos said Netflix’s underlying strategy remained unchanged, centred on exclusive, professionally produced series, films and live events, supported by licensing and global distribution.
“Our business and our business flywheel are working. There’s no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy. We do need better execution in the U.S.,” Sarandos said.
Notably, Netflix has posted monthly subscriber losses in the US throughout 2026, with no net additions reported ⁠for any month up to September, data from analytics firm Antenna showed, as reported by Reuters. Antenna tracks US subscription purchases via sources like credit card transactions, but excludes subscriptions acquired through wholesale bundles.
Sarandos acknowledged that the company had delivered “some really solid doubles and triples this year”, but said it needed more breakout hits that could travel internationally. “I know that we could do better,” he added, pointing to an opportunity to take the content slate to the next level.
Sarandos also highlighted the importance of creative talent, saying incoming chief content officer Peter Rice understood talent relations in a competitive market. Netflix recently laid off around 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce, and announced leadership changes involving content chief Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin.
Live sports and events remain central to the growth strategy. Sarandos said such programming can attract new members, support advertising revenue and increase value for existing subscribers. Yet competition from YouTube and TikTok, alongside questions over viewing-hour growth, puts greater pressure on Netflix to deliver stronger engagement.
The challenge now is to convert its global reach and content investments into faster growth, while improving advertising monetisation and maintaining profitability.
India is the example Netflix chose. View hours there grew 24% year over year in the third quarter, led by Lock Upp, its first daily reality series, according to the letter. Netflix recorded its largest quarter of paid net additions in India, and revenue there grew about 18% on a currency-neutral basis.

Netflix is set to report its third-quarter 2026 results after Tuesday's market close, with investors looking for signs that advertising growth and improving profitability can offset slowing revenue growth and intensifying competition from YouTube.

Revenue growth slowdown puts Q4 outlook in focus

For the third quarter, management guided for revenue of approximately $12.86 billion and earnings per share of $0.82, below previous Wall Street expectations.
The outlook triggered a sell-off after the company's previous results.
Revenue growth has slowed over recent quarters, falling from 17.6% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 16.2% in the first quarter of 2026 and 13.4% in the second quarter.
The third-quarter revenue guidance implies further deceleration to about 11.7%.
"Overall, we're not growing as fast as I want us to," co-CEO Ted Sarandos said recently at Bloomberg's 2026 Screentime event in Los Angeles.
"We are, though, also doing things that create a lot of headwind to that number," he added.
Investors will thus assess whether the company can stabilise growth or whether its expansion is slowing faster than anticipated.
The fourth-quarter outlook could prove particularly important.
Netflix's full-year 2026 revenue guidance stands at $51 billion to $51.4 billion.
Advertising growth offers a potential boost

While revenue growth has slowed, Netflix's operating margins have continued to improve.

The company's ability to control content costs while growing advertising revenue could help sustain profitability even as sales growth moderates.
Jefferies forecasts approximately 190 basis points of annual operating margin expansion through 2029.

Netflix is also undergoing organisational changes.

The company also announced plans on October 14 to cut approximately 1,000 jobs, or about 6% of its workforce, increasing scrutiny of cost discipline as content spending remains significant.
Recent analyst actions have reflected divided views on the stock.
Wells Fargo downgraded Netflix to Underweight in September, citing the possibility of declining viewing hours for its leading original programmes.
HSBC lowered its rating to Hold from Buy and cut its price target to $76.
Deutsche Bank subsequently upgraded the stock to Buy with a $95 target, while Goldman Sachs maintained its Buy rating with a $90 target.
KeyBanc, Morgan Stanley, Barclays and Huber Research have also lowered their price targets this month.
For Netflix, Tuesday's results will test whether advertising growth and margin expansion can offset slowing sales and heightened competition.
Investors will also look for signs that the company's international growth, pricing power and cash generation can sustain earnings expansion over the coming years.

Netflix keeps posting double-digit revenue growth while its stock craters toward a 52-week low, and the gap between Wall Street's most bearish and most bullish analysts has rarely been this wide. Something has to give, and the next earnings report…
Published October 16, 2026, 7:15am ET · 4 min read
© hocus-focus / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images
Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX | NFLX Price Prediction) currently trades at $72.61, while Wall Street’s average 12-month price target is $92.06. That gap implies 26.8% upside.
Netflix is still the largest subscription streamer, with an audience approaching a billion people and revenue up 13.4% last quarter. The most optimistic analysts see much more. The Street-high target of $135 implies 85.9% upside.
Netflix keeps growing while its stock keeps falling. Investors have to decide which side is right: the market’s worry about engagement or the analysts’ confidence in pricing power.
A Walked-Away Deal and YouTube’s Living Room Grab Sent Netflix Into a 39% Slide
Netflix’s biggest problem is attention. HSBC noted that YouTube captured a record 14.2% share of US TV time, while Netflix’s own view hours grew just 2% in the first half of 2026. The stock is down 22.56% year to date and 39.66% over the past year. That one-year decline is a severe drop for a profitable mega-cap.
Strategy confusion made it worse. Netflix declined to match a higher bid for Warner Bros. Discovery (NASDAQ:WBD) after calling the deal no longer attractive, and it collected a $2.80 billion termination fee. Earnings added pressure. First-quarter EPS of $1.23 missed the $1.345 estimate, and second-quarter free cash flow fell 32.73% to $1.53 billion on higher cash taxes.
Wall Street Trims Targets but Keeps the Buy Ratings
Recent revisions have been cuts to targets, while the ratings mostly held. Goldman Sachs reiterated Buy and lowered its target to $90, citing softer engagement and YouTube competition. Morgan Stanley also cut its target and still sees more than 40% upside. Wells Fargo issued a downgrade. Ratings still lean bullish: 7 analysts are most positive, 28 are positive, 15 are neutral and 1 are negative.
The bull case comes down to monetization. Netflix expects ad revenue to roughly double to about $3 billion, and its advertiser count grew 70% to more than 4,000 clients. Guidance calls for a 31.5% operating margin and roughly $12.5 billion in free cash flow. Netflix bought back $4.7 billion of stock last quarter, its largest buyback quarter ever, and still has $27.1 billion of authorization left.
The $135 case, associated with Pivotal Research and BofA Securities, argues that Netflix has won the global streaming wars outright. In that view, live sports and ad-tier growth bring in high-margin revenue. JPMorgan projects 24% annual EPS growth from 2025 through 2028. Consensus already expects EPS to rise from $3.5836 this year to $3.8087 next year. The first test is the upcoming earnings report, where management guided to $12.86 billion in revenue and $0.82 in EPS.
Disney and Roku Held Up While Netflix Fell Alone
This selloff is specific to Netflix. The rest of the streaming group has held steady or gained.
Walt Disney (NYSE:DIS) is down just 1.96% year to date at $110.66. Its average target of $126.49 implies 14.3% upside. Analysts are firmly bullish, with 29 Strong Buy or Buy ratings against 3 Holds and 1 Sell, but the targets point to a smaller gain than Netflix’s.
Roku (NASDAQ:ROKU) is up 42.57% this year at $154.67, close to its $162.33 target, which implies only 4.95% upside. With 20 Holds against 7 Buy-side ratings, analysts see the rally as mostly priced in.
Netflix carries the biggest analyst-implied upside among these peers. Targets are estimates and can be wrong, but this gap reflects worries specific to Netflix more than a sector-wide correction.
Netflix Lags the S&P 500 While Trading at 19x Forward Earnings
At $72.61, Netflix sits 26.8% below its $92.06 consensus target. The stock is down 22.56% so far this year, and the S&P 500 is up 13.18%. Over one year, Netflix has fallen 39.66%, compared with a 16.03% gain for the index.
Shares trade near the bottom of their 52-week range of $65.08 to $124.86, at 19x forward earnings.
Ad Growth and Engagement Will Decide Whether Netflix Closes Its Target Gap
Optimism grows if ad revenue reaches roughly $3 billion and margins hold near 31.5%. That would show pricing power can offset slower viewing growth. Heavy buybacks at these prices would add to per-share gains if the stock moves toward the consensus target.
The bear case gains weight if YouTube keeps gaining TV share and Netflix’s engagement growth stalls. That would turn the low multiple into a value trap. If engagement keeps slipping, future price increases will be harder to push through, and the $135 case depends on those increases.
The stock trades at 19x forward earnings for a company growing revenue by double digits, a multiple that sits near the low end of its 52-week range. The consensus target looks more realistic than the Street high, and the upcoming earnings report should show which side has the better read.

Netflix Inc.(NFLX) on Tuesday reported third-quarter earnings that beat Wall Street expectations, but its shares fell 5% in after-hours trading after the streaming firm issued a soft revenue outlook for the fourth quarter, setting it up for the fourth consecutive period of decelerating sales growth.
The company reported $12.9 billion in third-quarter revenue, matching Wall Street forecasts, and its earnings at $0.87 a share topped expectations of $0.82 a share.

Wall Street’s skepticism comes as the company works to reignite user engagement, scale its advertising layer, and adjust after failing to secure an acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery Inc.’s studio and streaming assets earlier this year.
Netflix has been struggling to consistently boost streaming revenue and new member additions over the past few quarters amid increasing competition from rival streaming services and is boosting programming of original content to ensure new additions.

Management Restructuring And Content Push
The earnings report follows a major operational overhaul led by Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters. Over the past week, Netflix announced a 6% workforce reduction—eliminating about 1,000 roles—its largest headcount cut since 2022.
In a bid to address perceived declines in programming quality and stagnant engagement, the company ousted Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin. To replace Bajaria, Netflix named Peter Rice, a seasoned industry executive who previously held leadership roles at both Walt Disney Co. and 21st Century Fox.
"With intense competition and an explosion of content competing for consumer attention, strategic clarity and excellent execution are critical," Netflix stated in its letter to shareholders, acknowledging that while core priorities are being met, "we see room to do even better."

Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, Netflix projects revenue of $13.4 billion, falling short of Wall Street estimates of $13.5 billion.
Netflix also projected a fourth-quarter operating margin of 26%, noting that severance and restructuring costs tied to its recent job cuts will weigh on profitability in the final three months of the year.
